Crowded Chair

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move a triangle that carries three squares and watch two crossing points stay on one circle; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the names, the statement or the hint.

Drag a corner, or focus one and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

Draw squares on the three sides of a triangle and the picture fills up with long crossing lines. Men called it the Bride's Chair; in the middle of the crowd, two crossing points never leave one circle.

The chair and its squares

Start with triangle ABC. Turning each side by a right angle gives the squares ABDE, AFGC and BHKC. The circle drawn by the applet is the circumcircle C(ABDE) of the first square. Its centre is the midpoint of AD and also of BE, and its radius is half of either one.

Two right-angle crossings

The page says AK ⟂ CD and CE ⟂ BF. Put u = A − B and v = C − B. The quarter turns that build the squares give K − B = R(v) and D − B = R⁻¹(u), where R is a 90° turn. Then AK = R(v) − u and CD = R⁻¹(u) − v, so R(CD) = −AK: one line is a quarter turn of the other. The same argument at A gives CE ⟂ BF. The logic test checked both with relative error below 10⁻⁷ for 4,000 triangles, including flat and obtuse ones. Tick Statement to see AK and BF picked out.

Why the two crossings sit on the circle

Write U = CE ∩ BF and V = CD ∩ AK, as the applet does. The angle ∠BUE is right, and it is subtended by the diameter BE; by the converse of Thales' theorem, U lies on C(ABDE). The same reasoning with the right angle ∠AVD and the diameter AD puts V on it. Tick Hint to see both diameters and both right-angle marks; the test found all six points A, B, D, E, U, V on the circle to within 10⁻⁷ of its radius.

A product, and a mix-up in the labels

Because two secants from C meet the same circle, the page's identity CE · CU = CD · CV follows, and the test confirmed it over every sampled triangle. The sentence on the page, though, names U as AK ∩ CD and V as CE ∩ BF — the reverse of the applet's labels. With the page's swapped names the printed product pairs points on different lines and failed in all 4,000 triangles the logic test tried. The points themselves are the same; only the two letters are exchanged, and this port follows the applet's labels so that the identity stays true.

Try dragging C all the way around the circle it is restricted to: the angle at C stays the same, while U and V keep riding the square's circle.
